title: AcmeAI x Redwood — tool calling + streaming deep dive (structured output guarantees)
summary: AcmeAI is building an agentic workflow that uses streaming chat completions with tool calling (multiple tools, sometimes in parallel) and wants schema-constrained JSON outputs for downstream automation. Team is confused about (1) how partial tool-call arguments arrive in the stream, (2) what constitutes the “final” assistant message vs tool-call messages, (3) whether Redwood guarantees valid JSON during streaming, and (4) how behavior varies by model family and OpenAI-compat mode. Redwood clarified the recommended mental model: treat streaming as a sequence of typed events; accumulate deltas for message content and tool-call arguments; only parse/validate structured output on the final assembled text; and implement retry/fallback when the model drifts off schema. Security questions focused on retention, audit logs, and running Dedicated vs Private/VPC for regulated data.
topics: Streaming event model (delta vs final assembly)
Tool calling payload shape and partial arguments
Parallel tool calls and ordering guarantees
Tool result messages and loop pattern (assistant -> tool -> assistant)
Structured output / JSON schema constraints and validation strategy
Security: logging, retention, VPC / Dedicated options
questions: Do you guarantee tool call arguments are complete and valid JSON at each streamed chunk?
When the model streams tool calls, is there a single tool_call_id we can rely on across chunks?
If the model emits multiple tool calls, can they be parallel and how do we correlate results?
Does “structured output” mean the response is always valid JSON, even while streaming?
What happens if the stream drops mid-tool-call (do we retry the whole request or resume)?
Is the payload shape identical to OpenAI, or are there differences we need to code for?
Can we force strict JSON schema adherence across all models?
action_items: Markus Klein: Send AcmeAI the canonical streaming + tool-calling example link (Python/TS/Go) and the 'known pitfalls' section (partial args, final assembly).
Ibrahim Khan: Share guidance snippet for accumulating partial tool arguments and deferring JSON parsing until a final event (include retry/backoff suggestion).
Wei Chen: Confirm which hosted models in AcmeAI’s target region have best tool-calling + structured output reliability, and send a suggested support matrix note.
Sarah Kim (AcmeAI): Provide one real tool schema + sample prompt and a failing transcript where JSON breaks, so Redwood can recommend model/prompt tweaks.
next_steps: Redwood to send follow-up email with runnable repo examples + docs pointers and a recommended implementation pattern for streaming tool calls.
AcmeAI to run a 1–2 hour spike using Redwood Hosted with their three key tools (search, profile lookup, ticket creation) and report where parsing breaks.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up the week of Feb 17 to review results and discuss Dedicated/VPC requirements with Security.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: AcmeAI x Redwood — tool calling + streaming deep dive (structured output guarantees)
Date: Feb 6, 2025
Time: 2:02pm–2:58pm PT
Duration: 56 minutes

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood, Solutions Engineering)
- Ibrahim Khan (Redwood, Staff SWE SDKs)
- Wei Chen (Redwood, Hosted API Docs)
- Sarah Kim (AcmeAI, Staff ML Engineer)
- Daniel Ortega (AcmeAI, Backend Lead)
- Priya Nair (AcmeAI, Security Engineer)
- Evan Brooks (AcmeAI, PM Agents)

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, I think we’re recording now. Um, thanks everyone for making time. The ask as I understand it is you’re already doing tool calling with streaming, and you want to understand what’s guaranteed, what’s not, and what we recommend so you’re not… like, chasing edge cases.

[00:17] Sarah Kim: Yep. We have an agent loop, we’re streaming, and we’re seeing tool arguments come in like half-JSON, and then our parser explodes. So we need to know what we should be doing.

[00:28] Daniel Ortega: And also how we handle multiple tools. Because sometimes the model tries to call two things at once, and our code isn’t sure what to do.

[00:35] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Ibrahim is here because he’s been leading parity across SDKs, and Wei from docs. We can go deep and also align on what we want to show in public examples.

[00:47] Evan Brooks: Great. And just to set context, we’re evaluating you versus… well, we have OpenAI in prod for one flow, and we’re prototyping on Bedrock too. But we want to use open models long term, and we’re trying to avoid rewriting our whole agent harness.

[01:03] Markus Klein: Got it. Before we dive: what deployment mode are you aiming for? Hosted first, then dedicated, or straight to VPC?

[01:10] Priya Nair: Security will likely push VPC if any customer PII is in prompts. But we can start hosted for evaluation if retention is short and we can control logs.

[01:20] Markus Klein: Okay. Hosted can be configured with limited retention and you can redact client-side. For VPC/Private we can get into later.

[01:30] Ibrahim Khan: On the technical side, the big thing to internalize is streaming is not “a sequence of valid JSON objects.” It’s a sequence of events, and some events contain fragments, like deltas, that aren’t parseable until you assemble them.

[01:44] Sarah Kim: That’s exactly the confusion. The model is calling a tool, arguments are streamed, and our JSON parser expects a whole object.

[01:52] Ibrahim Khan: Right. So in our canonical pattern, tool-call arguments are treated as a string buffer. You append partials as they come in. Then you only parse once you get a terminal indicator, like a final event, or the tool-call is marked complete.

[02:10] Daniel Ortega: Is that a Redwood thing or just like… generally with these models?

[02:14] Ibrahim Khan: Generally. And different providers expose it differently. In OpenAI you might see tool_call arguments accumulate in deltas too. If you parse on each chunk, you’ll lose.

[02:26] Wei Chen: We’re updating docs to be explicit about this. The old snippets in the wild kind of implied arguments were complete each time, which isn’t true.

[02:36] Sarah Kim: So what are the event types? Like, what should we key off?

[02:41] Ibrahim Khan: In our SDKs we expose a stream iterator of events. You’ll typically see: message.delta for content tokens, tool_call.delta for tool-call fields, and message.final when the assistant message is complete. Names vary slightly per SDK but the mental model is the same.

[02:58] Daniel Ortega: Wait, do you send a separate “tool_call.final”?

[03:02] Ibrahim Khan: Depending on the model and adapter, you may see a final-ish event per tool call, but we don’t want people to rely on that. Our recommendation is: track tool calls by an id, accumulate deltas, and consider the assistant turn complete when the assistant message final arrives.

[03:20] Sarah Kim: The tool_call_id is stable across chunks?

[03:23] Ibrahim Khan: Yes, within a single streamed response. That’s the stable key. If the model emits multiple tool calls, they’ll have different ids.

[03:32] Daniel Ortega: And ordering? Like if tool A’s args stream, then tool B, then back to tool A?

[03:38] Ibrahim Khan: It can happen. Not super common, but you should code defensively. The safe approach is: maintain a map tool_call_id -> buffer. Append deltas to the correct one.

[03:52] Markus Klein: That’s one of the “known pitfalls” we’re adding. Folks assume a single tool call at a time.

[04:01] Evan Brooks: We also care about parallel calls. We’d like the model to call, say, “search_docs” and “get_user_profile” in the same turn.

[04:09] Ibrahim Khan: Two parts there. The model can output multiple tool calls in one assistant turn. Whether you execute them in parallel is up to you. Our docs will show a pattern where you can run them concurrently and then send tool results back as separate tool messages, one per tool_call_id.

[04:27] Daniel Ortega: So we send back multiple tool results before asking the model again?

[04:31] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. The loop is: assistant requests tools -> you execute tools -> you append tool-result messages -> you ask the model for the next assistant turn.

[04:44] Sarah Kim: Okay. Now structured output. We want the final assistant response to be JSON that matches a schema. And we want to stream because we show partial progress in UI.

[04:55] Sarah Kim: Do you guarantee valid JSON during streaming?

[04:58] Wei Chen: Important nuance: we can guide the model using a schema and our structured output mode, but we don’t claim every partial chunk is valid JSON. The guarantee is about the final assembled output meeting constraints—depending on model support.

[05:13] Sarah Kim: So “structured output” is not “every token is valid JSON” basically.

[05:18] Wei Chen: Correct.

[05:20] Ibrahim Khan: And even the final output is probabilistic. Some models are very reliable; others will occasionally drift. So you should validate and retry when invalid.

[05:32] Daniel Ortega: That’s… not super satisfying. We were hoping it’s like hard-constrained.

[05:37] Markus Klein: Totally get it. There’s a spectrum. Some models have strong constrained decoding or better function calling reliability. But we still recommend validation.

[05:47] Evan Brooks: On OpenAI we have a bunch of guardrails and retries too. We just want to know what we’re signing up for.

[05:54] Ibrahim Khan: The practical guidance: if you need JSON for automation, you validate against JSON Schema. If invalid, you retry with a correction prompt. If you can’t retry (latency), you fall back to a non-streamed call or a smaller model that’s more consistent, depending on your policy.

[06:13] Sarah Kim: What does the schema look like in your API?

[06:16] Wei Chen: In the request you provide a schema object. In docs we show a pattern: type object, required fields, additionalProperties false, and explicit enums where possible. The tighter the schema, the fewer failure modes.

[06:34] Daniel Ortega: If we set additionalProperties false, does the model actually respect it?

[06:39] Ibrahim Khan: Often yes, but it’s model dependent. It’s not like a compiler. Again: validate.

[06:47] Sarah Kim: We got failures where it returns JSON but with trailing commentary. Like, “Here you go: { ... }” and then some text.

[06:56] Wei Chen: Yep, common. The best mitigation is: instruct “output must be valid JSON only” and use schema mode. And then your parser should reject extra text.

[07:09] Daniel Ortega: But we’re streaming. We want to show partial JSON in UI.

[07:13] Ibrahim Khan: For UI, you can show the raw streamed text, but don’t parse incrementally unless you’re using a tolerant incremental parser, and even then it’s tricky. Most customers display it as text while streaming and only treat it as JSON on final.

[07:29] Sarah Kim: So we should not do incremental JSON parsing?

[07:32] Ibrahim Khan: Not as your core correctness path. You can attempt it for UX, but the “truth” should be final assembly + validation.

[07:41] Markus Klein: And we’ve seen support cases where folks parse at 200ms intervals and then blame the model. It’s just partial data.

[07:49] Priya Nair: From security perspective: are those partials logged anywhere on your side?

[07:54] Markus Klein: For hosted, you can configure data retention and logging. We can also talk about redaction. For Private/VPC, logs stay in your environment. Wei, do you want to cover specifics?

[08:06] Wei Chen: Generally, hosted supports configurable retention and audit logs for enterprise tiers, and we can disable storing request/response bodies. Metadata like latency and token counts remains for billing and diagnostics.

[08:19] Priya Nair: Okay, we’ll need the SOC 2 and the exact retention knobs, but that’s separate.

[08:25] Markus Klein: Noted.

[08:28] Daniel Ortega: Back to tool calling. We also saw “arguments truncated” mid stream. Like the JSON closes early. Then the model proceeds.

[08:37] Sarah Kim: Yeah, it’s like it started a string and never finished it.

[08:41] Ibrahim Khan: That’s a real edge case. Sometimes the stream disconnects. Sometimes the model deviates. Implementation-wise you should detect invalid JSON on tool arguments at the moment you’re about to execute the tool. If invalid, you can either ask the model to re-emit the tool call, or you can retry the whole assistant turn.

[09:03] Daniel Ortega: How do we know it’s “about to execute the tool” though? Like, do we wait for final?

[09:08] Ibrahim Khan: If the assistant message indicates tool calls, you’ll typically stop and execute tools once you’ve received the complete tool-call argument string for each tool. In practice, that’s at the end of the assistant turn. So yes: wait for final, then parse args, then execute.

[09:25] Sarah Kim: That means we can’t start executing tools while the model is still talking?

[09:30] Ibrahim Khan: You can, but it adds complexity. Some customers do speculative execution once a tool args JSON becomes parseable, but if it changes later you’ve got a mess. The safest is execute after final.

[09:46] Evan Brooks: We care about latency, though. We want tool calls to start quickly.

[09:50] Markus Klein: Understood. There’s a tradeoff: latency vs correctness. A common compromise is: if you’ve received a syntactically complete JSON object for a tool call and you haven’t seen any more deltas for that id for, say, 200–300ms, you can start. But you still need rollback logic.

[10:12] Daniel Ortega: That’s what we were afraid of.

[10:14] Ibrahim Khan: For first iteration, don’t do speculative. Get it correct first.

[10:20] Sarah Kim: Okay. What about the payload shapes. We want to be OpenAI compatible, meaning we can swap providers.

[10:28] Ibrahim Khan: Redwood supports an OpenAI-compat endpoint, but there are differences in streaming event names and sometimes in where fields appear. We’re actively documenting those diffs so examples don’t imply perfect parity.

[10:45] Wei Chen: We’ll send you a link to the compatibility notes. The big gotchas: partial args streaming, tool call indexing, and final message assembly.

[10:56] Sarah Kim: So your “canonical” Redwood SDK interface is not exactly the OpenAI one.

[11:02] Ibrahim Khan: Correct. Our native SDKs expose a normalized event model. The compat endpoint tries to mimic OpenAI’s shape, but you still need to handle deltas similarly.

[11:16] Daniel Ortega: Got it.

[11:18] Markus Klein: Can we get specific about your agent? What tools, what schema, what success criteria?

[11:24] Evan Brooks: Sure. Three tools: search_docs(query, top_k), get_user_profile(user_id), and create_ticket(title, body, severity). The model does triage: it reads user request, searches docs, then creates a ticket if needed.

[11:41] Sarah Kim: And for structured output, we want the final result to be like {"resolution": ..., "actions": [...], "ticket": {...}} with strict enums.

[11:52] Ibrahim Khan: Perfect. That’s exactly the kind of schema that works well.

[11:56] Daniel Ortega: Our current prompt says “return JSON”, but it still sometimes wraps it in markdown.

[12:02] Wei Chen: We’ll recommend you specify “no markdown, no code fences” and use schema mode.

[12:10] Sarah Kim: What models do you recommend for tool calling reliability? We tried a couple open models elsewhere, tool calling is… shaky.

[12:19] Markus Klein: We can suggest a starting point, but I don’t want to over-promise. Wei can send the current matrix.

[12:27] Wei Chen: In hosted, we have a handful of models we’ve profiled for tool calling and structured output behavior. Some are better at argument formatting; some are better at schema adherence. We’ll share what we can publicly, and for anything sensitive we’ll do it in a follow-up.

[12:45] Sarah Kim: Is there any setting like “strict mode”?

[12:48] Ibrahim Khan: There’s schema-guided generation. But “strict” still requires validation. Think of it as increasing the probability of a valid response.

[12:58] Daniel Ortega: Understood.

[13:01] Priya Nair: On retries: if we retry the same request, are we billed twice?

[13:06] Markus Klein: Yes, usage-based. Some teams implement client-side idempotency keys and only retry on certain failure types. We can discuss best practices.

[13:17] Sarah Kim: If the stream drops mid-response, can we resume?

[13:22] Ibrahim Khan: Not resume at a token boundary. You’d re-issue the request. But you can do it safely if you track conversation state and you make tool executions idempotent.

[13:34] Daniel Ortega: So we need to avoid double-creating tickets.

[13:37] Ibrahim Khan: Exactly. Add an idempotency key to create_ticket, or check for existing ticket by external_id.

[13:46] Evan Brooks: That’s fine.

[13:49] Markus Klein: Can we walk through a concrete streaming transcript? Like what your consumer loop should do.

[13:55] Sarah Kim: Yes please.

[14:00] Ibrahim Khan: Okay, imagine the assistant decides to call search_docs. In the stream you’ll get events like: tool_call.delta with name “search_docs” and then a series of tool_call.delta events with arguments fragments: “{\"query\": \"how do i reset” then later “ password\", \"top_k\": 5}”. Your code appends.

[14:22] Ibrahim Khan: Separately, you might also see assistant content deltas like “Let me check the docs…” depending on the model. Some models mix narrative with tool calls.

[14:33] Daniel Ortega: That mixing is annoying.

[14:35] Ibrahim Khan: Yep. In an agentic workflow, we usually instruct the model to not produce user-facing narrative during tool call turns. But not all models comply.

[14:46] Wei Chen: We’re adding doc guidance: for tool calls, prefer a system instruction like “When calling tools, do not emit additional text”.

[14:56] Sarah Kim: Do you support a mode where assistant content is suppressed when tools are requested?

[15:01] Ibrahim Khan: Not as a server-side guarantee. It’s prompt discipline.

[15:06] Markus Klein: Some customers do post-processing: ignore assistant content when tool_calls exist.

[15:12] Daniel Ortega: That’s probably what we’ll do.

[15:14] Ibrahim Khan: After you get message.final, you now have a list of tool calls with complete args. You validate args JSON; if valid, execute tools; then you send tool results back as messages of role “tool” with tool_call_id. Then ask the model for the next turn.

[15:34] Sarah Kim: In our code, we were executing as soon as we saw the tool name.

[15:38] Ibrahim Khan: That’s the source of truncation errors and parse errors.

[15:43] Sarah Kim: Makes sense.

[15:45] Evan Brooks: How do you recommend representing tool results? Some providers want like a string.

[15:51] Ibrahim Khan: Tool results are usually strings, but in our SDKs you can send JSON-stringified results. The key is consistency: the model needs a predictable shape.

[16:03] Daniel Ortega: If we have two tools, do we send two tool messages then one assistant request?

[16:09] Ibrahim Khan: Yes. Or you can interleave: tool result, assistant, tool result, assistant. But the simplest is: send all tool results, then request the assistant.

[16:22] Sarah Kim: That implies the model sees results for all tools at once.

[16:26] Ibrahim Khan: Correct.

[16:28] Markus Klein: And you can control parallelism in your executor. Like run search and profile concurrently.

[16:36] Evan Brooks: Great.

[16:38] Priya Nair: Quick question: audit logs. If we’re sending tool results that contain PII, is that stored?

[16:44] Wei Chen: On hosted, by default we don’t need to store content. We keep operational metadata. For enterprise, we can provide audit logs of access and config changes. For Private/VPC, you control storage.

[16:57] Priya Nair: Okay.

[17:00] Sarah Kim: Back to structured output. We want the final assistant answer after tools to be schema compliant. What’s the best failure handling pattern?

[17:08] Ibrahim Khan: The pattern is: 1) request with schema, 2) on final, attempt JSON parse and schema validate, 3) if fails, send a corrective turn: “Your previous output was invalid because X; output valid JSON only that matches this schema.” Limit retries to 1–2.

[17:29] Daniel Ortega: And if it still fails?

[17:31] Ibrahim Khan: Fallback: run a repair step (extract JSON substring) or switch to a more reliable model for that step.

[17:41] Sarah Kim: Do you provide a built-in repair helper?

[17:44] Wei Chen: Not as a product feature, but our examples include lightweight helpers. We’re trying to keep it copy/paste.

[17:53] Markus Klein: We can send a snippet. It’s basically “find first { and last }” but with caveats.

[18:00] Sarah Kim: That hack scares me.

[18:03] Ibrahim Khan: It should. It’s a last resort. Better is retry with a correction prompt.

[18:10] Evan Brooks: What about function calling vs structured output? We’re mixing both.

[18:15] Ibrahim Khan: Think of tool calling as structured output with a special schema: the model emits a list of calls. Then after you run tools, you can request structured JSON output for the final answer. Just keep the steps separate.

[18:31] Daniel Ortega: Got it.

[18:33] Markus Klein: Are you doing streaming for the final structured JSON step?

[18:37] Sarah Kim: Ideally yes, for UX. But we can accept non-streamed for that part if it’s more reliable.

[18:44] Ibrahim Khan: That’s a common choice: stream the “thinking / narrative” in user-facing chat, but for the machine-readable final artifact, use non-streamed or at least validate only at the end.

[18:58] Sarah Kim: We don’t show chain-of-thought, but we show progress like “Searching… creating ticket…”. That can be separate from the model response.

[19:06] Markus Klein: Exactly. You can drive progress indicators off your tool execution rather than streaming JSON.

[19:13] Daniel Ortega: That’s helpful.

[19:15] Sarah Kim: One more thing: when the model streams tool call arguments, are they always JSON? Like could it be something else.

[19:23] Ibrahim Khan: The arguments are intended to be JSON object, but models can output invalid stuff. So treat it as untrusted until validated.

[19:33] Sarah Kim: So no guarantee.

[19:35] Ibrahim Khan: No absolute guarantee.

[19:38] Evan Brooks: And what’s Redwood’s position on “guarantees”? Like what can we tell our stakeholders.

[19:45] Markus Klein: You can say: the platform supports schema-guided structured output and tool calling, with best-practice patterns and SDK examples; correctness is achieved with validation + retry; and we provide observability for failures. We don’t promise zero invalid outputs.

[20:03] Daniel Ortega: That’s fair.

[20:05] Wei Chen: We’re also trying to be careful with terminology. Not “JSON mode” like some vendors say, but “structured output” with schema constraints, with documented model support.

[20:17] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[20:19] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about OpenAI compat. Are you using their Assistants API style or chat completions?

[20:25] Daniel Ortega: Chat completions style. Tools are in the request.

[20:30] Ibrahim Khan: That maps well. In Redwood native SDKs, the naming might differ, but conceptually same.

[20:39] Daniel Ortega: We had a TypeScript type mismatch in a sample we found. Tool results didn’t typecheck.

[20:46] Wei Chen: Yeah, we’ve seen that. We updated types recently. We’ll make sure you’re using the current snippet.

[20:55] Sarah Kim: Also the event names. We saw “chunk” vs “delta” vs “event”.

[21:01] Ibrahim Khan: Yep. We’re standardizing. The internal standard is: you get events with a type, and a payload. “delta” means partial. “final” means assembled complete.

[21:15] Markus Klein: And the docs will match across Python/TS/Go.

[21:21] Sarah Kim: Cool.

[21:23] Priya Nair: Last security thing: data residency. We need US-only.

[21:28] Markus Klein: Hosted supports US regions. Dedicated can be region-pinned. Private/VPC obviously in your cloud.

[21:37] Priya Nair: Great.

[21:39] Evan Brooks: What about logging tool calls and results in the console? We don’t want PII in dashboards.

[21:45] Wei Chen: You can configure to show minimal content, or disable content logging. The console focuses on token counts and latency. For deep debugging you can opt in, but we’ll align on your policy.

[21:59] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[22:01] Markus Klein: Can I ask, what are your latency requirements?

[22:05] Daniel Ortega: For the triage flow, under 3 seconds p95 end-to-end would be ideal, but with tools it’s probably more like 5–7.

[22:15] Markus Klein: Okay. Then speculative tool execution might matter later, but we’ll start with correctness.

[22:23] Sarah Kim: Agreed.

[22:25] Ibrahim Khan: One more edge case: sometimes tool-call args include unicode or escaped quotes. If you’re concatenating strings, make sure you don’t double-escape. Append raw deltas as provided.

[22:39] Daniel Ortega: We were doing JSON.stringify on each delta…

[22:43] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah, don’t. That will break.

[22:47] Sarah Kim: That explains some stuff.

[22:50] Wei Chen: We should add that to pitfalls.

[22:53] Markus Klein: We will.

[22:55] Evan Brooks: So what do you recommend we do this week to evaluate?

[23:01] Markus Klein: I’ll send a runnable example that includes: streaming tool calls, parallel tool execution, and then a final structured JSON output with schema validation and retry. You take your three tools and swap them in.

[23:17] Sarah Kim: Great.

[23:18] Markus Klein: And if you can, send us one failing transcript where args were truncated or JSON invalid. Ibrahim can suggest how to handle.

[23:28] Sarah Kim: Yep.

[23:30] Priya Nair: And I’ll follow up separately on SOC 2 and retention config.

[23:35] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[23:37] Daniel Ortega: Do you have guidance on tool result size limits?

[23:41] Ibrahim Khan: Keep tool results small. If search_docs returns big chunks, summarize or return ids and fetch later. Big tool results increase latency and can degrade the next model step.

[23:56] Sarah Kim: We currently return the top 5 passages fully.

[24:00] Ibrahim Khan: That might be too big. Consider returning snippets + doc ids. Or compress.

[24:08] Evan Brooks: We can adjust.

[24:10] Markus Klein: This also ties to cost.

[24:13] Daniel Ortega: Yep.

[24:15] Sarah Kim: One last question: if the model emits two tool calls, but we only want one, can we restrict it?

[24:22] Ibrahim Khan: You can set tool_choice = required vs auto, and in some interfaces specify a specific tool. But if you want “at most one tool call,” it’s mostly prompt instruction. Some models will still emit multiple.

[24:37] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[24:39] Wei Chen: We’re adding a doc note: don’t assume single tool call; handle list.

[24:44] Sarah Kim: Great.

[24:46] Markus Klein: Anything else before we recap?

[24:49] Evan Brooks: No, this was good.

[24:51] Priya Nair: I’m good.

[24:53] Daniel Ortega: Same.

[24:55] Markus Klein: Cool. Recap: streaming tool args come in partials, don’t parse until final; correlate by tool_call_id; support multiple tool calls; execute tools after final for correctness; structured output is schema-guided but validate + retry; don’t expect valid JSON mid-stream; and we’ll send updated examples and compatibility notes.

[25:18] Markus Klein: Next steps: I’ll send links today. Sarah will send failing transcript. We’ll schedule a follow-up week of Feb 17 to review your spike and talk deployment/security.

[25:30] Sarah Kim: Sounds good.

[25:32] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

---

Auto-generated Notes (Fireflies)
- Action items captured above.
- Key risk: customer currently parses tool-call arguments incrementally; needs buffer + final-parse pattern.
- Key confusion: “structured output guarantees” interpreted as always-valid JSON during streaming; clarified it applies to final output and is model-dependent.
